opinions.rationale: The residual problem is real: data fitness is specific to the protocol, estimand, and decision context, and prespecified component-level no-go criteria would improve study governance. The statement nevertheless overstates the absence of quantitative assessment. Availability, temporal resolution, treatment support, follow-up continuity, outcome capture, and validation performance can all be measured, although they do not collapse into a universally valid score. External validation data are not required for every fitness component. A pipeline without explicit stop rules also does not necessarily always return an estimate, while an estimator's standard error generally will not represent bias from nonidentification or poor measurement. Benchmark concordance cannot by itself validate a fitness score because disagreement can arise from estimand differences, transportability, adherence, measurement, or bias in either study. This is decision-critical when an essential protocol component is unobservable or unsupported; otherwise, standardized scoring and publication of assessments are primarily governance and reproducibility improvements.
opinions.weakest_true_restatement: Many target-trial emulations lack prespecified, protocol-specific quantitative adequacy criteria and no-go rules. Transparent component-level assessments could improve decisions about whether to proceed, but thresholds must be estimand- and decision-specific, and randomized-trial concordance alone cannot validate them.

opinions.rationale: The central warning is correct: operational differences can make site-specific estimates contrasts for different populations, interventions, outcomes, or follow-up regimes. A pooled result is still mathematically an average under specified weights, but it is not automatically an effect for a scientifically meaningful target population. Heterogeneity statistics cannot identify whether variation reflects effect modification, sampling error, positivity problems, or semantic mapping failure. The impossibility claim is too strong, however. Patient-level centralization is not required for all relevant diagnostics; sites can return cohort attrition, prevalence, support, balance, event rates, code-set provenance, and other privacy-preserving summaries after local validation. Conversely, sufficient statistics, influence curves, and balance summaries are not enough to establish semantic equivalence. A transport model also cannot repair incorrectly defined variables and requires explicit target-population and effect-modification assumptions. The open problem is reliable semantic validation and governance under federation, not the complete absence of diagnostics.
opinions.weakest_true_restatement: Federated pooling can silently combine operationally distinct site-specific estimands unless variable semantics, target populations, and pooling weights are explicit. Heterogeneity alone cannot distinguish mapping failure from effect modification, although local validation and privacy-preserving aggregate diagnostics can flag some incompatibilities without centralizing patient records.

opinions.rationale: It is technically correct that a common data model standardizes representation without guaranteeing semantic, measurement, or causal equivalence. Versioned provenance and temporal validation are therefore important. Several stronger assertions are not generally correct. Semantic drift is not necessarily invisible in an analytic dataset; prevalence discontinuities, distribution shifts, coding transitions, and changes in associations can flag it, although provenance is usually needed to explain it. Linkage error is not inherently nonrandom and should not generically be called confounded measurement error: depending on the linkage mechanism, it can induce selection bias, exposure or outcome misclassification, or little bias. Most importantly, carrying probabilistic linkage weights into a causal estimator does not automatically convert hidden bias into interval width. That requires a calibrated linkage model, compatible integration with treatment and censoring estimation, and valid uncertainty propagation; differential or misspecified linkage can leave substantial bias. Provenance graphs, drift checks, and leave-one-source-out analyses are useful diagnostics but cannot prove semantic invariance or identify linkage bias by themselves. The issue is critical when key eligibility, treatment, confounder, or outcome variables are affected, but otherwise may be a robustness and provenance roadmap item.
opinions.weakest_true_restatement: Common data models do not by themselves guarantee semantic equivalence. Versioned provenance, temporal checks, and linkage sensitivity analyses can reveal some failures, and uncertain linkage should be propagated under explicit assumptions; probabilistic linkage weights alone do not guarantee unbiased estimation or turn all linkage bias into variance.
